output.name: Sekúla

anatomy.part: apex of the kite, its head at the top of the sail
end of the tail, where the streamers hang
the bow of the cross-spar, at the centre of the sail
bridle knot just below the spine

output.myth: When Aun cut the string he did not cut it clean. The last of it hung from the Sun-Kite's tail, and Ennu the Kite-Wright sewed the Sun-Kite from old sailcloth so it could be flown along the Lamp Road by day. Each evening Hesk reels it in, and each morning it goes up again, which is why the sun seems to rise. But once the Gale Tavo took the bridle in his teeth and tore one knot loose. The head went one way and the tail the other, and the stars Tálun and Tirsa are where they are because of it. Aun laughed when he saw it, then he was sorry, and he has been sorry since. Sil still walks the shore looking for his string. If you see a kite going up at dusk, do not call out to it. It may be carrying a dead man's name up to the Spindle, and it will need all its line to get there.
